questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: explain why the postwar system replaced the earlier rules
questions.stem: Between 1931 and 1934 governments facing depression cut the value of their own currencies, raised tariffs, and took trade from each other, so world trade shrank. In 1944 the leading financial powers rewrote that rule. Which rule, and what was it meant to stop?

options.text: Fixed rates, so no state could devalue to steal demand

options.misconception: confuses the postwar order with the alternative it rejected
options.text: Free floating, so each market found its own level daily

options.misconception: invents a currency board no conference created
options.text: One world currency, managed by a single finance ministry

options.misconception: misses the change the conference made to the old system
options.text: The old gold standard, with its prewar rules left unchanged

questions.explanation: The lesson of the 1930s was that a state which cut its currency and its tariffs could pull exports at a neighbor's expense, and the new rules removed that freedom by holding each currency steady, so recovery had to come from moving goods rather than from undercutting a rival. The tempting answers name the two systems actually rejected, a floating rate and a single currency, or a gold standard left exactly as it had been.
questions.hint: Which freedom had let one state undercut its neighbors?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: identify what made one currency the reserve asset
questions.stem: The postwar monetary system made one currency the one in which reserves were held and debts settled, and its issuers could exchange it for a fixed weight of metal as long as they had metal to pay. Which currency filled that role, and what made it possible?

options.text: The United States dollar, backed by the largest gold holdings

options.misconception: ignores that wartime sales had shrunk those reserves
options.text: The British pound, whose gold reserves were the largest then held

options.misconception: invents a currency the conference declined to create
options.text: A new supranational currency issued by the 1944 conference

options.misconception: treats a defeated state's currency as a reserve asset
options.text: The German mark, restored when the old empire's gold came home

questions.explanation: The dollar became the pivot because the United States held most of the world's monetary gold and the largest economy to trade with, and holding reserves in the currency of the biggest creditor meant a country could settle with anyone. The tempting answers rely on reserves that had been spent in war, on a currency nobody issued, or on gold that had left the country as reparations.
questions.hint: Which country had both the gold and the buyers?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two rival plans at the 1944 conference
questions.learningObjective: analyze how rival designs became two institutions
questions.stem: Read the record: at the 1944 conference one delegation proposed an institution that would lend long-term to rebuild war damage, another insisted the new system needed a currency exchangeable for metal on demand, and the compromise put both under one roof. What does that record show about how the postwar order was built?

options.text: That rival plans were merged into institutions with separate jobs

options.misconception: misses the compromise the record describes
options.text: That the two delegations had agreed one identical plan

options.misconception: inverts which side gained the currency piece
options.text: That the metal exchange was dropped to please the lenders

options.misconception: reads a completed bargain as an adjournment
options.text: That the conference postponed all decisions to a later meeting

questions.explanation: The conference settled less by choosing one idea than by putting rival ideas under separate headings, so the lending institution rebuilt economies while the currency institution supplied the reserve asset, and each program then made the other more credible. The tempting answers report agreement, a dropped clause, or a deferral, and the record shows a working bargain carrying two mandates.
questions.hint: How many jobs did the final arrangement carry?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The domestic bargain behind the fixed rates
questions.learningObjective: analyze how two commitments were held at once
questions.stem: Governments that promised full employment and cheap credit at home also had to hold their currencies steady abroad, and the record shows them accepting both obligations at once. How could the two commitments be held together?

options.text: By taxing and spending within limits that kept the rate credible

options.misconception: assumes the domestic pledge was quietly dropped
options.text: By giving up the promise of full employment after 1945

options.misconception: confuses the bargain with automatic price rises
options.text: By letting wages rise with prices so workers kept real buying power

options.misconception: treats unlimited borrowing as a source of credibility
options.text: By borrowing abroad to defend the rate whatever the cost

questions.explanation: A currency held steady abroad is kept there by the promise that it will not be changed at home, so tax and spending restraint became the price of the fixed rate, and a government wanting both had to deliver growth without the inflationary relief a devaluation would have given it. The tempting answers each drop half of the bargain or substitute a device that does nothing for the rate abroad.
questions.hint: What does a fixed rate ask of a government at home?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first trade agreement bound
questions.learningObjective: identify the design that made a tariff cut permanent
questions.stem: In 1947 a group of countries signed an agreement that cut their tariffs in exchange for cuts from one another and bound the result so it could not be raised at will. What did that design give the world that it had not had before?

options.misconception: confuses bound rates with a uniform rate
options.text: One common tariff rate applied by every participating country

options.misconception: assumes an external tariff the agreement never had
options.text: A customs union with a single tariff on outside goods
A negotiated reduction that both sides were held to

options.misconception: invents an escape clause that undid the binding
options.text: A right for any member to raise its tariff when industry suffered

questions.explanation: A tariff cut a government may reverse by decree is a favor rather than a bargain, and binding each side to the level it negotiated is what let firms plan investment around the lower rate for decades. The tempting answers convert the agreement into a common rate, a customs union, or a loose arrangement, and each drops the binding that was the whole point.
questions.hint: What made a cut different from a favor?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A decision rule for a club of a hundred
questions.learningObjective: design a rule that keeps a large club from stalling
questions.stem: A trade club of more than a hundred governments decides only by consensus, the largest members could block any change, and the small members fear being bound by rules they did not write. Which rule change most keeps the club working?

options.text: Let members propose changes that bind those who accept them

options.misconception: makes the club safe for large members and empty for others
options.text: Give the largest members a standing veto over every proposal

options.misconception: preserves the veto that is causing the stalemate
options.text: Require the same vote from every member before any rule binds

options.misconception: assumes rules can bind a state that never consented
options.text: Let decisions take effect without any government's agreement at all

questions.explanation: A club of a hundred governments will never agree on everything, so a rule that lets like-minded states proceed without waiting for unanimity keeps the agreement growing while leaving any state free to stay out, which is the arrangement that has held for decades. The tempting answers either confirm the veto that causes the paralysis or bind states that never consented, and the second destroys the agreement's legal base.
questions.hint: How do you keep growing without needing unanimity?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a regional market was built
questions.learningObjective: explain the certainty a regional arrangement provided
questions.stem: When European governments removed tariffs among themselves they also set one external tariff and common rules for goods, capital, and workers, and several later made the same arrangement with former colonies. Why build a regional bloc if world trade was opening?

options.text: To gain the certainty of a market without waiting for world terms

options.misconception: inverts a customs union into a barrier for outsiders
options.text: To stop trade between members and keep it inside the region

options.misconception: invents a command authority the treaties withheld
options.text: To give the largest member a veto over every customs law

options.misconception: removes the single external tariff a union requires
options.text: To let each member set its own external tariff alone

questions.explanation: World negotiations moved at the pace of the most reluctant participant, and a bloc let governments settle terms among themselves where the stakes and the politics were their own, then bargain as a group from that stronger position. The tempting answers make the union a barrier, a command structure, or a set of independent external rates, and each misses the certainty the arrangement was built to deliver.
questions.hint: Who sets the pace when a hundred countries negotiate?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Trade creation and trade diversion
questions.learningObjective: analyze the two effects a preference can produce at once
questions.stem: Read the record: two governments abolish tariffs on each other's goods and set one external tariff, and afterward a buyer in the second country pays more for a car from a third country than before, while a buyer in the first pays less for a machine from the second. What does that pair of results show about such an agreement?

options.misconception: assumes a uniform gain with no loser named
options.text: That abolishing tariffs lowers prices for every buyer

options.misconception: treats a diversion as evidence of a legal fault
options.text: That the higher car price proves the union's rules were illegal
That removing barriers inside can create trade and divert it

options.misconception: reads an internal gain as evidence on the external rate
options.text: That the cheaper machine shows the external tariff was too low

questions.explanation: Inside the union the tariff on the partner's goods disappears, so trade grows where barriers were high, and outside it the common external tariff can exceed what either government had applied, so some trade is pulled away from third suppliers, and one arrangement produces both effects. The tempting answers insist the outcome must be uniform, or read a change in internal prices as a verdict on the external rate.
questions.hint: What happens to a third country outside the union?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two lending mandates
questions.learningObjective: identify which institution answered which problem
questions.stem: Two institutions were set up in the 1940s: one was to hand out short-term currency to members whose payments were in trouble, the other to lend for rebuilding and later for development. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: The fund for temporary needs, the bank for long-term loans

options.misconception: swaps the two institutions' stated purposes
options.text: The fund for rebuilding ports, the bank for weekly needs

options.misconception: merges the mandates and invents a size limit
options.text: Both for rebuilding, the fund limited to the smallest members

options.misconception: collapses the two into one and adds a structure
options.text: Both for short-term currency, the bank run by a committee

questions.explanation: The two were separated by the length of the problem they answered, since a country out of foreign currency needed help within weeks while a country with bombed railways needed help for years, and merging them would have let urgent claims exhaust the funds meant for building. The tempting answers swap the mandates or combine them, and either would mix a cash crisis with a capital program.
questions.hint: How long did each kind of problem take to fix?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The export structure inherited at independence
questions.learningObjective: explain what did not change when sovereignty did
questions.stem: A state that became independent in 1960 found four fifths of its export earnings came from one crop, that its mills imported most of what they consumed, and that its trade ministry's staff had been trained by the former colonial power. What had not changed at independence?

options.text: The shape of the economy the colonial power had built

options.misconception: supposes the tariff code was rewritten from nothing
options.text: The laws that regulated how goods entered the country

options.misconception: moves the legacy to finance rather than production
options.text: The currency in which the state's debts were still counted

options.misconception: suggests a list survived but the economy did not
options.text: The names of the firms holding the largest export licenses

questions.explanation: Sovereignty changed who signed the treaties while the ships, the plantations, the warehouses, and the trained civil service stayed in place, so a new flag sat on top of an economy built to send raw material out and bring manufactures in, which is why flag and structure were independent. The tempting answers suppose the tariff code, the currency, or the license list survived while the production base did not.
questions.hint: Who kept running the ports and the plantations?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why one commodity hurts one state more
questions.learningObjective: analyze why equal price shocks produce unequal losses
questions.stem: Two states sell the same single commodity into one world market. The first has a wide manufacturing base and can hold output up when the world price falls; the second has no other export and must sell whatever it has. Why do they not suffer equally from one price fall?

options.misconception: attributes resilience to a currency arrangement
options.text: Because the first state's currency answers to a lender

options.misconception: explains the difference in wages rather than earnings
options.text: Because the second state's farmers were paid a smaller share

options.misconception: invents a second price series the record lacks
options.text: Because the world price of manufactures fell twice as far
Because only the second state has no second source of income

questions.explanation: A price fall in one commodity cuts export earnings only for a country that has to sell that commodity, and only the second does, so the first absorbs a worse price with factories still earning while the second must sell at any price to buy the fuel and spare parts it lacks. The tempting answers move the difference to a lender, to wages, or to a second price series, and the record shows none of them.
questions.hint: Which state has something else to sell?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A currency that outlived the colony
questions.learningObjective: analyze how monetary sovereignty lagged political sovereignty
questions.stem: Read the record: after independence the finance ministry issues notes in its own name, a merchant's contract still states payment in the old colonial currency, and the new central bank keeps its reserves and its rate decisions tied to the currency across the sea. What does that arrangement show?

options.misconception: reads the record as the opposite of a new issue
options.text: That the new state had abolished its own currency at once

options.misconception: invents foreign control of the printing plant
options.text: That the former power ran the printing press of the state

options.misconception: treats the contracts as void instead of honored
options.text: That trade contracts were void for naming a dead currency
That monetary independence lagged well behind the flag

questions.explanation: A currency is a promise that a government will honor it at a rate it controls, and if reserves, contracts, and the exchange rate are still decided across the sea, the new state has changed the name on the notes without changing who stands behind them, so monetary sovereignty is a separate step from independence. The tempting answers invert the record, invent a printing control, or treat honored contracts as void, and the merchant's contract proves the opposite.
questions.hint: Who still decides the exchange rate?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why emergency loans carried conditions
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism behind a policy condition
questions.stem: A member in payments trouble borrows from the fund and is told it must cut its budget deficit, raise taxes, and open its currency before the money arrives. Why did the lenders attach these conditions?

options.text: Because the reserve is shared, so one member's use drains it

options.misconception: misstates the institution's charter
options.text: Because the fund was chartered to regulate domestic budgets

options.misconception: invents a deposit rule the fund never had
options.text: Because no member could lend without a security deposit

options.misconception: borrows the wrong institution's mandate
options.text: Because the money was meant only for rebuilding destroyed ports

questions.explanation: The fund's money came from every member, so a borrower that spent it unrestrictedly would be using other countries' reserves to postpone its own adjustment, and the conditions are the device that keeps one country's emergency from becoming a shared cost. The tempting answers rewrite the fund as a budget regulator, a lender to secured borrowers, or a reconstruction agency, and each drops the pool of shared money that requires any condition at all.
questions.hint: Where did the money in the fund come from?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve asset created in 1969
questions.learningObjective: identify the shortage a new reserve asset addressed
questions.stem: By the late 1960s countries were short of the currency the system needed for settling with each other, and in 1969 a new kind of reserve was created that no government had to earn first. What problem was that meant to solve?

options.misconception: mistakes a liquidity shortage for a metal shortage
options.text: A shortage of metal in the vaults of the largest holders

options.misconception: treats the reserve as a commodity supply
options.text: A shortage of goods to exchange for the old reserve asset

options.misconception: assumes holders were unwilling rather than short
options.text: A shortage of countries willing to hold the old reserve
A shortage of the means to settle between countries

questions.explanation: The new reserve answered a settlement shortage, since a country that owed more than it held had to find dollars or metal before it could pay anyone, and the new holding let members draw against future need instead of earning each payment in advance. The tempting answers relocate the shortage to metal, to goods, or to willingness, and the system was short of none of those three.
questions.hint: What must a debtor have before it can pay anyone?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the gold link was cut in 1971
questions.learningObjective: explain why a promise had to be abandoned
questions.stem: The postwar system held each currency at a fixed weight of metal, and the country that supplied the reserve currency spent abroad more than it earned, so by 1971 its metal no longer covered what other countries held. What had to give?

options.text: The link between the reserve currency and metal on demand

options.misconception: thinks fresh metal would restore the old cover
options.text: The metal standard, saved by finding and mining more gold

options.misconception: blames the drain on aid rather than on trade
options.text: The foreign aid programs, which caused the whole imbalance

options.misconception: blames a deficit on tariffs, which cut imports
options.text: The tariff schedules, which had raised the trade deficit sharply

questions.explanation: A promise to exchange metal on demand is credible only while the metal is there, and a reserve currency's obligations grow with the world's appetite for it, so the issuing country eventually owed more than it could deliver and the link had to be cut rather than the promises kept. The tempting answers each find a repair or a culprit that leaves the promise in place, and one of them misreads what tariffs do to imports.
questions.hint: For how long can a promise to deliver outlast the stock?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency after floating
questions.learningObjective: interpret a usage share as evidence of position
questions.stem: A decade after the metal link was cut, a survey of central banks finds that most of the world's reserves and a large share of international invoices are still settled in one currency, and that the country issuing it has the largest economy. What does that pattern show?

options.misconception: reads continuity as a restored convertibility rule
options.text: That the metal link was quietly restored at a new rate

options.misconception: replaces a reserve share with a trade ranking
options.text: That the issuing country had become the largest exporter

options.misconception: misreads invoiced trade as barter agreements
options.text: That invoice settlement had been replaced by barter deals
That a currency's role rests on size and habit, not metal

questions.explanation: Once the metal promise was gone the currency kept its place because every other holder already held its obligations and needed somewhere to settle, and depth of that kind does not switch off when a rule does, so the figure measures a position rather than a legal privilege. The tempting answers turn a usage share into a restored rule, an export ranking, or a barter system, and the survey reports none of them.
questions.hint: What holds a reserve in place once a rule is gone?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1973 rise in the price of oil
questions.learningObjective: identify what a price change redistributed
questions.stem: Late in 1973 suppliers raised the price of crude roughly fourfold, and within months the buying states had bills that outran their reserves while the selling states held surpluses they had never had. What had changed most in one year?

options.text: The distribution of income between buyers and sellers

options.misconception: confuses a price change with a quantity change
options.text: The world supply of oil, which the new prices cut sharply

options.misconception: invents a producer count the year did not see
options.text: The number of countries producing oil, which had doubled

options.misconception: redirects the change to a source left untouched
options.text: The share of fuel the buyers took from domestic wells

questions.explanation: The quantity of oil barely moved that year, so what changed was the price, and a price paid by nearly every industrial state to a handful of producers transfers purchasing power between them rather than removing energy from the world. The tempting answers each change something other than the price, and a shortage, a doubling of producers, or a domestic supply surge would have appeared in quantities rather than in bills.
questions.hint: Did the world run out of fuel in 1973?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the years after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: interpret a price and output pair as a cost shock
questions.stem: A table for the years after the oil rise shows consumer prices climbing faster than wages, factories working below capacity, and unemployment rising, all at once, where the previous decade had shown the opposite pairing. What does the combination tell you about the shock?

options.misconception: assigns the cause to budget policy
options.text: That it came from governments spending more than they took in

options.misconception: reads the effect as the cause
options.text: That demand collapsed after the price rise and emptied the factories

options.misconception: moves the cause to wage setting instead of costs
options.text: That workers' wage claims were all set before the rise began
That it was a cost the economy could not pass on

questions.explanation: Prices up with output down is the signature of a cost the economy could not pass on, and an oil price set abroad is exactly such a cost, because raising taxes or cutting spending would have removed demand the slump had already weakened. The tempting answers treat the price rise as a demand story, whether from spending or from wages set in advance, and falling orders are what rules that out.
questions.hint: Which direction were prices and output moving?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Recycling the oil revenue through the banks
questions.learningObjective: analyze a financial circuit as a transfer of income
questions.stem: Read the record: the oil states deposited much of their new revenue in banks in the United States, those banks lent it onward to governments and firms elsewhere at high rates, and the money came back to the oil states as deposits and loans to their own banks. What does that circuit show?

options.text: That the payment moved income without creating new wealth

options.misconception: confuses a financial circuit with a trade surplus
options.text: That the oil states had become the largest goods exporters

options.misconception: moves the circuit to a legal change of 1971
options.text: That the United States had ended its own currency limits

options.misconception: claims the opposite of what the deposits show
options.text: That the oil states had stopped buying from the borrowing states

questions.explanation: The circuit shows a transfer, not a creation: the importing states paid the bill, the exporting states received it, and the banks standing between passed it on as credit, so the world had the same money circulating at a higher rate and through a longer chain than before. The tempting answers convert a financial flow into a goods surplus, a legal restoration, or a collapse in trade, and the record describes none of them.
questions.hint: Did the circuit produce anything new, or move something?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second oil rise and the repricing of debt
questions.learningObjective: explain how a second cost rise became a solvency problem
questions.stem: The importers' bills were still high when suppliers raised prices again, and central banks then raised rates until borrowing cost roughly doubled, and firms that had borrowed at the earlier rates stopped paying. How do the three facts fit together?

options.misconception: blames a withdrawal of credit on the oil states
options.text: Borrowers failed because the oil states stopped lending

options.misconception: substitutes a currency event for the rate rises
options.text: Firms failed because the currency they owed in was devalued

options.misconception: reports a stop the record contradicts
options.text: Trade stopped because the importers could buy no fuel
Debt written at old rates was repriced by a second rise

questions.explanation: Rates rose to defend currencies and to answer a second rise in import bills, and that repriced debts written when money was cheap, so firms that had merely borrowed to build met payments set by a world they could not vote in, which is how an expensive year became a solvency problem. The tempting answers locate the failure in a credit withdrawal, a devaluation, or a complete halt in trade, and the record shows none of them.
questions.hint: What does a rate rise do to a loan signed earlier?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why two sectors stayed outside the rules
questions.learningObjective: explain the distributional bargain behind the exclusions
questions.stem: From the start the trade rules were written for manufactured goods, and the two sectors employing the poorest farmers and the most low-wage workers were left out of them. What kept those sectors outside for decades?

options.text: The importers of those goods had more at stake than the gains

options.misconception: invents a timing story the record contradicts
options.text: Those goods did not exist when the rules were first drafted

options.misconception: misstates the negotiation rule as a requirement
options.text: The rules required every product to be treated the same each year

options.misconception: attributes the exclusion to a lending decision
options.text: The lending institution had ruled those sectors unprofitable

questions.explanation: Removing a barrier helps the member most in the goods it imports, and the largest importers had their own farmers and workers behind those tariffs, so giving up textiles and farm goods to keep manufactures open was the price of the whole system rather than an oversight. The tempting answers explain the exclusion by timing, by a technical requirement, or by a lending judgment, and none of those is a reason to keep a tariff in place.
questions.hint: Which side of a tariff line gains most when it falls?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the last round had to be one package
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a long deadlock broke in a single bargain
questions.stem: For twenty years a handful of countries refused every attempt to bring farm goods and services under the rules, and when the talks of the late 1980s finally concluded, every sector had been traded away inside one sealed agreement. Why could the deal only be struck that way?

options.text: Each side would surrender a sector only for a gain elsewhere

options.misconception: confuses the negotiating method with the amendment rule
options.text: The rules could be amended only by a unanimous vote of all

options.misconception: claims the sectors were struck from the agreement
options.text: Farm goods and services had been removed from the charter

options.misconception: reads the package as a device for imposing rates
options.text: One package let the largest members impose their own rates

The tempting answers turn a negotiating method into a voting rule, a deletion, or an imposition, and the method is what made the concessions defensible.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why disputes needed a referee both sides obeyed
questions.learningObjective: explain why a remedy must sit with someone other than the injured party
questions.stem: The older trade rules had no panel to hear a complaint and no ruling to appeal to, so a country that felt cheated could only answer with its own tariffs, and in practice most never did. What did the newer procedure add?

options.text: A panel whose ruling both sides were required to follow

options.misconception: invents a damages remedy the procedure lacks
options.text: A private court that awarded cash to the complaining country

options.misconception: substitutes a ranking exercise for a hearing
options.text: An annual vote in which all members ranked each other

options.misconception: grants the answer the procedure replaced
options.text: A license for either side to shut its market any time

questions.explanation: A remedy only the injured party may use is a remedy nobody uses, because using it makes the complainer the aggressor, so the newer system took the choice away from the complaining country and made a ruling both had to follow, which is what finally made complaints worth filing. The tempting answers add damages, a vote, or a license for unilateral closure, and each leaves the decision with the injured party, which is the flaw being removed.
questions.hint: Why did nobody use the old remedy?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concentrated gains and diffuse costs
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a beneficial law still needs compensation
questions.stem: When a tariff on machinery falls, the producers who gain are few and identifiable while every consumer pays a little, and when a tariff on rice falls the reverse is true. Why did governments need compensation schemes to pass such laws?

options.misconception: says the concentrated losers were voiceless
options.text: The losing producers had no power to object at all

options.misconception: makes the obstacle a measurement problem
options.text: The gains could not be measured before the law took effect

options.misconception: narrows the issue to one revenue line
options.text: The lost tariff revenue had to be replaced by income tax
The losses are spread widely and the gains concentrated

questions.explanation: A law that helps a small visible number while costing a large invisible one is easy for the few to block and easy for the many to overlook, so giving the visible losers something back changes the arithmetic in every chamber that votes on it. The tempting answers deny the losers any power, turn the problem into measurement, or reduce it to a single revenue line, and the politics turns on who is organized rather than who is right.
questions.hint: Who notices a loss of a few cents?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: From import substitution to export orientation
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a development strategy reversed direction
questions.stem: A state first replaced imports with domestic factories behind high tariffs, and when its debts and its foreign exchange shortage grew it cut those tariffs, courted foreign firms, and built for export instead. What drove that switch?

options.misconception: invents a legal ruling as the cause
options.text: A ruling that made the protective tariffs legally impossible

options.misconception: supplies a disaster the record does not show
options.text: A famine that destroyed the factories built under protection

options.misconception: makes a world price the cause of the switch
options.text: A fall in the world price of the goods it had imported
The first policy consumed the currency the second earned

questions.explanation: Manufacturing imports behind tariffs pays for machinery in the currency the state is trying to earn, so the reserves drained faster the better the policy worked, and once bills and debts outran earnings, exports became the only route to the currency that buys fuel and parts, which is why the second policy aimed at the same account from the other side. The tempting answers supply a legal bar, a disaster, or a world price the record does not contain.
questions.hint: In which currency were the imported machines paid for?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the export composition of a growing region
questions.learningObjective: interpret export shares as evidence of the growth source
questions.stem: Between 1960 and 1985 the manufactured share of one region's exports rises from a tenth to more than half, while its own market for manufactures stays small and the share of those exports made by foreign-owned plants also rises. What do the three figures together indicate?

options.misconception: contradicts the small home market in the table
options.text: That the region had built a large home market for its output

options.misconception: reads foreign ownership as evidence of local firms
options.text: That domestically owned factories supplied the new exports

options.misconception: claims a substitution the shares do not show
options.text: That the exports displaced the region's primary commodity sales
That the growth came from selling into foreign demand

questions.explanation: Manufactures leaving the region in that quantity cannot have gone mostly to buyers at home, so the growth is explained by foreign demand met at low labor cost, and the rising foreign-owned share says a growing part of that production was somebody else's decision to locate it there rather than the local state's own. The tempting answers contradict one of the three figures each, and the figures are consistent with one another.
questions.hint: Where did those manufactured goods actually go?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a default on a foreign currency loan
questions.learningObjective: analyze how a devaluation enlarges a foreign debt
questions.stem: Read the record: a government borrows for five years at a rate near eight percent, fuel prices double, the lenders then charge about eighteen percent, the currency devalues, and the government stops paying and asks to negotiate. Why does the devaluation enlarge the debt rather than shrink it?

options.misconception: invents a legal rewriting nobody ordered
options.text: A devaluation legally requires every existing loan to be rewritten

options.misconception: reverses which side's currency moved
options.text: The lenders' own currencies fell as fast as the debt

options.misconception: claims a home loan the record excludes
options.text: The government had borrowed only in its own currency at home
The bill is fixed in a currency the borrower must earn

questions.explanation: A foreign currency loan is a promise to deliver a quantity of that currency, so when the borrower's own currency falls the same local sum buys fewer units and the bill has to be met with more exports, and the devaluation meant to help exports thereby enlarges the obligation rather than reducing it. The tempting answers make the devaluation a legal event, a synchronized fall, or a currency mismatch the record excludes.
questions.hint: In which currency is the promised payment fixed?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first defaults revealed about lending
questions.learningObjective: identify the pricing error a default exposed
questions.stem: A handful of countries stopped paying, lending to the rest dried up within a year, and the rate on the loans that remained rose. What did those defaults reveal about the way the loans had been priced?

options.misconception: claims the borrowers were hopeless from the start
options.text: Those borrowers had never been able to pay from the beginning

options.misconception: overstates a credit freeze as an insolvency
options.text: The lenders themselves had gone bankrupt in a quarter

options.misconception: denies a practice the record describes
options.text: No other country had ever borrowed in a foreign currency
The whole category had been priced as a single risk

questions.explanation: Lenders had treated widely used borrowers as one class and priced the class, so a few who could not pay made the rest look alike in the only way that matters to a balance sheet, and the drying up of credit to solvent borrowers shows the rate had been set for an average that no longer existed. The tempting answers make the event an insolvency, a hopeless class, or a currency practice nobody avoided.
questions.hint: What did the rate assume about the next borrower?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Financing aid without taxing what it builds
questions.learningObjective: design a levy that does not penalize success
questions.stem: A ministry wants a program that raises export earnings in a country whose average income is three hundred dollars a year, and it proposes funding the program with a levy on the exports it hopes to raise. Which design least builds dependency?

options.misconception: widens the levy without moving it off exports
options.text: Spread the levy wider so every producer pays a visible share
Fund it from a broad base that falls as output grows

options.misconception: makes the burden temporary but keeps it on exports
options.text: Keep the levy for a fixed term, then review it every year

options.misconception: rewards output while leaving the tax on exports
options.text: Charge the levy only after targets are met, to reward success

questions.explanation: A levy on the earnings the program is meant to raise makes the state's own success a reason for the cost to grow, so a broad base with a rate that declines as output climbs lets the program finance itself without taxing the thing it was built to grow, which is what keeps the recipient working toward the target. The tempting answers all keep the charge attached to exports while describing the arrangement as sound policy.
questions.hint: What does the program tax when it taxes its own target?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a trade bargain everyone will sign
questions.learningObjective: design terms each party can defend at home
questions.stem: Two large economies and one small one are writing a trade agreement, and the large ones have the most to lose from opening while the small one has the most to gain. What most improves the odds that all three sign?

options.misconception: puts the first cost on the party with most to lose
options.text: Promise the largest member the first cut to show good faith

options.misconception: removes the defense the small party needs at home
options.text: Keep the terms secret until the small party has ratified them
Give the small party a share it can defend at home

options.misconception: hands the strongest party a one-sided exit
options.text: Let the largest member revise the schedule after five years

questions.explanation: A government signs what it can defend at home, so the small party needs a visible gain worth defending before it will bind itself, and giving it that share costs the large parties less than losing the whole agreement to a walkout over terms they could have traded. The tempting answers front-load the concession to the party with least at stake, hide the terms from the one that must sell them, or write a revision only the strongest can use.
questions.hint: Who has to persuade voters to sign?
